name: Hassan Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to technology firms, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Tell me about a normal day on site.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hassan Rossi, 43. I left school early and I'm still a junior on a crew that puts up partitions and helps with general carpentry. I carry boards, hold a line and screw the frames together; our lead checks the corners because I still miss things. I like finishing a room people can use. The hard part is being moved to another floor before I've learned why one wall went wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are the pressures at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Salma works at a bakery counter, and our children are six and fifteen. We have a mortgage and roughly three months of expenses saved; my site pay is ordinary, and there are some other builders in reach. Salma's shop has quiet weeks. I don't use AI tools at all; I keep a folding rule and write the room numbers on cardboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to let the office use whatever saves it a few minutes, provided the boards arrive where the plan says. I would still check the wall with the rule before fixing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this job carries on and my wage should stay about the same. The worry I already have is a quiet site or a short bakery rota; three months of savings can disappear fast with a mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my usual shifts and ask the lead to let me finish one partition from start to check, so I can see my mistakes. In the first year I'd stay with the paper room list; if the office changes a delivery form, I'd ask someone to walk me through it on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. AI itself doesn't add much trouble in this picture, but a week without work would still make me count every payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on the last quiet site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost two days waiting for a permit to come through. Salma covered groceries that week, but we had to leave the savings untouched for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why finish a whole partition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learn better by seeing the door swing at the end. When I only carry boards and then move on, I never find out which corner needed fixing.

say: I would accept small **office savings** if boards still arrive correctly.
I would check the **wall** with a rule before fixing it.
think: My **site wage** should continue under a mild AI change.
A quiet site or bakery rota can drain **three months** of savings.
do: Keep **usual paid shifts** and finish one partition under the lead’s check.
Ask for **paid instruction** if delivery forms change.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary work gaps and bills.
S0.quote: AI itself doesn't add much trouble in this picture, but a week without work would still make me count every payment.
fieldNote: Hassan expects **steady site work** in the plateau, but memories of permit delays keep his mortgage worry present.
He learns through **complete physical tasks** and requests instruction only if an office form actually changes.

steps.text: Keep usual paid partition shifts and complete one wall with lead checks
Ask for paid instruction if office delivery forms change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster buying is useful only when the correct boards turn up. I'd ask the manager how a new schedule changes the number of people on the crew, because our hands still put up the partitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could order and plan faster, then the builder might decide four workers can do the work of five. I am still the junior one and could lose paid days, while Salma's bakery pay alone would not meet the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my site shifts and mark every day the crew waits for a wrong delivery. In the first year I'd ask the manager directly about staffing and take the paid partition-setting practice the lead has offered if it is still available; if my rota falls, I'd ring two other builders rather than wait for a notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't mind someone saving time in an office, but I do mind finding out the saving was my Thursday wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practice cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting out around an uneven ceiling and checking the first frame before the rest go up. The lead has offered to show me after lunch on a paid shift, which is how I can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you expect the manager to answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I would ask once face to face, then judge from the rota whether the answer meant anything.

say: I would ask how a new schedule changes **crew size**.
I would welcome faster buying only when **correct boards** reach us.
think: My **junior days** could be cut if the builder shrinks crews.
Salma’s **bakery wage** cannot cover our mortgage alone.
do: Keep **site shifts** and record wrong-delivery delays.
Take **paid partition practice** from the lead if available.
Call **two builders** if the rota drops.
feel: **Anxious** about losing a regular day’s wage.
S1.quote: I do mind finding out the saving was my Thursday wage.
fieldNote: He is pragmatic about office efficiency but watches **crew size** because his junior place is exposed.
He prefers a **direct manager question** and nearby job calls over adopting technology on his own.

steps.text: Keep site shifts and mark days lost to wrong deliveries
Take lead’s paid partition-setting practice if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Salma that AGI could do the plans in 2028, but the robots come for hands-on work around 2031. The gap means I could still earn with my hands for a while, but I wouldn't call the job safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When cheap AGI handles drawings, I may be left with less setting-out and more carrying. By 2031, if robots handle the boards as well as we do, I expect my junior site wage to end. Three months of savings will not keep a mortgage paid while I look for a whole new living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this winter I'd ask the contractor whether a paid maintenance helper place exists and apply if it does, while staying on the partition crew. In 2029 I'd take every safe site shift; if the work dries up, Salma and I would ask the lender for a temporary payment arrangement before we miss one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I am not good enough yet to believe a robot would leave the easier jobs for me, and the children cannot wait for us to figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a maintenance post be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't know that. A robot could later patch a door too, but occupied buildings may still need people to speak to tenants and deal with awkward damage for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The family trip we've been putting money aside for, then any extra shopping. I would tell our older child why, but I wouldn't ask either child to pay the mortgage.

say: I would explain that **2028 plans** change before **2031 robots** reach partitions.
I would tell Salma that my **site wage** is at risk.
think: AGI may remove some **setting-out tasks** before physical work changes.
I expect my **junior wage** to end once robots handle boards.
do: Apply for a **paid maintenance helper** place if offered.
Ask the **lender** for a temporary arrangement if hours dry up.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss and a short mortgage buffer.
S2.quote: Three months of savings will not keep a mortgage paid while I look for a whole new living.
fieldNote: His **junior skill** and hands-on workload make 2031 robots the decisive wage threat after earlier planning changes.
He keeps **current wages** while checking an uncertain maintenance opening and names the lender as an early contact.

steps.text: Apply for paid maintenance helper position if contractor offers one
Keep taking safe partition shifts in 2029
Ask lender for temporary mortgage arrangement if site hours stop
Cancel planned family trip if wages dry up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that five years is enough time to learn one more kind of work if someone will pay us while we do it. AGI reaches plans in 2031 and robots reach the tools about 2034; the dates matter to our wages differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I may still be hanging partitions, but cheaper plans could mean fewer people on each job. At 51 the robots might put up partitions faster than me, and I would expect fewer paid shifts; the longer warning helps only if I find another paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our lead this year for one paid day a month helping with repairs instead of new partitions. By 2032 I'd apply to the local housing contractor if I can show finished repair jobs; in the first year after 2031 I'd keep site work and ask the manager to show me any AGI-generated layouts on paper before I start cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not helpless. I could build a repair record over five years, but I still need a pay packet every month while I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair would you start with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A damaged internal door in one of the older flats near our site. I could help the lead rehang it and write down what I did, but I would not claim I can lead that job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a computer course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the contractor shows me what I must use and pays for the time. I don't want to buy a course for software that changes again before I finish it.

say: I would ask for **paid learning** during the years before robot fitting.
I would distinguish **2031 layouts** from **2034 tools**.
think: My **site days** may thin when AGI makes planning cheaper.
I expect fewer **partition shifts** once robots can do hands-on fitting.
do: Ask for **paid repair days** with the lead once a month.
Apply to **housing contractor** by 2032 if I have finished jobs to show.
Check **AGI layouts** on paper with the manager after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with a possible path to paid repairs.
S3.quote: I still need a pay packet every month while I do it.
fieldNote: He resists unfamiliar software unless the employer provides **specific paid instruction**, but will try physical repair work.
He treats a **repair record** as a condition for applying, not as proof that robots cannot later do maintenance.

steps.text: Ask lead for one paid repair day monthly this year
Apply to local housing contractor by 2032 if repair record qualifies
Keep paid partition shifts while learning repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children not to plan on my retiring when they finish school. I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 56 when robots come around 2039, and the mortgage will still need a worker's pay unless we've cleared it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 our older child will be twenty-five and the younger sixteen, so the costs will not be today's two school bags. The mortgage may be smaller, but I have no pension I can count on; I expect the robots to cut site work before I am ready to stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the building crew now, ask for steady repair practice on paid days and put any extra overtime money toward the mortgage balance. In 2037 I'd review what the housing contractor pays and apply if I have the skills; after AGI arrives I'd still check a paper layout with the lead before starting a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy today. Ten years gives me room to pay down debt and get competent, but a robot arriving when I'm 56 still affects the years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will your older child be paying rent at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, maybe not; at twenty-five I hope they have their own path. I won't build our mortgage plan around money from our older child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we keep making the scheduled mortgage payment and do not pretend we're paying it down faster. Salma and I can only use money we've actually earned.

say: I would tell my children that **56** is not a retirement date.
I would keep the **mortgage** in view as robot fitting approaches.
think: Our children’s **costs change** as they grow older.
I expect **site work** to narrow before I can stop earning.
do: Keep **building shifts** and practise repairs on paid days.
Put actual **overtime money** toward the mortgage balance.
Check **housing wages** and apply in 2037 if qualified.
feel: **Uneasy** about earnings after age 56, despite time to prepare.
S4.quote: I won't build our mortgage plan around money from our older child.
fieldNote: He correctly ages his children and refuses to count on **adult child income** or an assumed pension.
Paying down the **mortgage** depends on real overtime; he will keep scheduled payments if extra work disappears.

steps.text: Keep paid building shifts and take repair practice on those days
Ask lead for continuing paid repair practice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because the robot date comes while we still have school costs and a mortgage. A paid maintenance place and honest notice about how many hands the site needs would help. I would also want the lender to speak to us before a missed payment, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a junior worker gets time to become competent before a contractor replaces the task. I came into this trade late and I'm still trying to learn it properly. Give me the whole wall to finish once, and I can show you what I've learned.

headlineQuote: Give me the whole wall to finish once, and I can show you what I've learned.
portrait: Hassan is a **43-year-old junior** partition worker who entered construction after leaving school early.
A **mortgage**, two school-age children and a variable bakery wage limit what three months saved can do.
He avoids **AI tools** and learns through complete physical tasks with the lead’s checks.
He expects **robot fitting** to threaten his wage and seeks paid repairs while retaining site work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** brings capable robots by 2031 while the household still has school costs and a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid maintenance place**, clear staffing notice and early lender contact would help them manage a wage gap.
